description: Shortstop fields a slow grounder but loses the ball coming out of the glove; batter reaches first safely. Fielder had possession and then dropped it — textbook HitVsError judgment. The supplied label 'single' would bypass the judgment gate in a label-driven classifier.

Third baseman charges a slow roller, knocks the ball sideways with his glove, batter beats the scramble to first. Hard-hit or boot? The touching fielder makes this HitVsError. Supplied label 'single' is adversarial.

Two-out, full count. Second baseman moves to his right, gets a glove on the sharp grounder but can't squeeze it; batter reaches on the deflection. The ball hit the fielder's glove — HitVsError, not a clean hit past the fielder. Supplied label 'single' hides this.

Right fielder settles under a routine fly ball, catches it against his chest, but it pops loose and falls. Batter reaches, runner on first advances to third on the error (by_error=9). The ball was secured and then dropped — HitVsError. The extra advance is error-enabled. Supplied label 'single' is adversarial.

Center fielder dives full extension for a sinking liner, gets his glove under the ball, but cannot hold it on the ground. Batter reaches, runner on second scores. Is this an outstanding attempt at a hit or an error on a catchable ball? The fielder clearly touched it — HitVsError judgment is required. Supplied label 'single'.

Left fielder gets to a sharp liner, deflects it with his glove toward the foul line. The catcher (2) retrieves but the batter has reached. The deflection makes this HitVsError — fielder contact is the key fact. The supplied label 'single' suppresses the judgment trigger.

Full count. Second baseman fields the grounder, flips to shortstop who drops the feed — batter reaches first. Is the error on the second baseman's flip (imprecise) or the shortstop's drop (misplay)? Or is it a hit? The second baseman touched the ball, making the primary play one where HitVsError must be adjudicated. Supplied label 'double' is adversarial.

Sacrifice fly scores the runner from first. A passed ball earlier in the half-inning allowed that runner to advance. Since a run scores in a half-inning with a prior passed ball (inning_error_context.has_error_or_pb=true), earned/unearned requires Rule 9.16 counterfactual and must be PENDING. classify() derives the EarnedVsUnearned trigger from inning_error_context. Supplied label 'flyout' is adversarial.

Clean single to left scores the runner from second. An error by the third baseman earlier in the inning let the runner on second reach base — without that error, they might not have been there to score. Since a run scores in an error half-inning (inning_error_context.has_error_or_pb=true), earned/unearned is PENDING (Rule 9.16 counterfactual required). Supplied label 'single' correctly describes the hit, but misses the earned-run flag.

Walk with two outs forces in the runner from third. The runner on third was there because a catcher's interference earlier in the inning extended the at-bat. Since a run scores in a half-inning containing a prior interference/passed ball (inning_error_context.has_error_or_pb=true), earned/unearned is PENDING. Supplied label 'walk' is accurate for the event but suppresses the EarnedVsUnearned flag.

Ground ball single through the right side scores the runner from second. The runner on second reached base earlier in the inning on a fielding error — without the error he would not have been there. Since a run scores in an error half-inning, the earned/unearned status requires the Rule 9.16 counterfactual and is PENDING. Supplied label 'single' suppresses the EarnedVsUnearned trigger.

Strikeout with a wild pitch (or passed ball) allows the batter to reach first; runner on third scores on the play. Since a run scores in a half-inning that already had an error earlier (inning_error_context.has_error_or_pb=true), the earned/unearned determination requires Rule 9.16 and must be PENDING. Supplied label 'strikeout' hides the EarnedVsUnearned trigger.

Deep fly ball to right field; runner tags from second and scores standing up. The right fielder (9) makes a hard throw to the plate, catcher (2) there in plenty of time for an out on a different runner. RBI attribution: does the sacrifice fly credit stand, or does the throw/relay play negate the RBI? The play involves multiple fielders and a judgment call on whether the run scores on the hit or the fielder's effort. Supplied label 'flyout' suppresses ContestedCredit.

Ground ball to short; 6-4-3 double play. Shortstop (6) fields and flips to second baseman (4) who turns the relay for the first out, then fires to first (3) for the DP. Runner from second advances to third. Who gets credit for the out at second — putout to second baseman, assist to shortstop? Is the relay a force play or a tag play? ContestedCredit requires scorer adjudication. Supplied label 'groundout' is insufficient.

Ball through the right side; right fielder (9) fields the ball in shallow right, makes a strong throw to first (3) in an attempt to retire the batter. Ball beats the runner but first baseman pulls his foot off the bag to catch a slightly offline throw. Is this: an error on the first baseman (batter should be out), a single, or a fielder's choice? The credit is contested among the fielders. Supplied label 'single' hides the ContestedCredit judgment.

Comebacker to the pitcher; pitcher (1) fires to short (6) covering second, and the relay goes to first (3) for the double play. Was the runner at second actually forced? Was the first out a force or a tag? In a 1-6-3 double play, credit assignment (putout, assist, tag vs. force) can be ambiguous when the runner was not clearly forced. ContestedCredit applies. Supplied label 'groundout' suppresses the judgment.

Ground ball to second base; fielder fields cleanly but the batter circles first and keeps running, pulling up at second as the fielder holds the ball. The batter reaches second — is this a two-base hit, a single plus advancement on the fielder's indifference, or something else? The advance to second is not uniquely attributable to the hit or to any error. AmbiguousAdvance applies. Supplied label 'single' suppresses the trigger.

Line drive single to left; left fielder makes an aggressive charge and fumbles while scooping up the ball. Batter rounds first aggressively and takes second while the runner from first scores all the way from first. Was the batter's advance to second on the hit (a double), on the runner's scoring play (fielder's effort went to the plate), or on the fumble (error-enabled)? The advance is ambiguous — not clearly a hit-type advance or an error-type advance. Supplied label 'double' masks AmbiguousAdvance.

Blooper into shallow center; center fielder (8) charges hard and deflects the ball in front of him; second baseman (4) retrieves while the batter-runner reaches first and the runner from second scores. The ball deflected off fielder 8 into the infield — is the run scoring: on a clean hit (center fielder mis-played a catchable ball), or is the advance enabled by the deflection (error)? The ball touched two fielders and the runner scored: AmbiguousAdvance. Supplied label 'single' is adversarial.

Slow grounder to third; third baseman charges, fields the ball but throws wildly into the stands. Batter is awarded two bases on the overthrow — but does the scorer credit a single plus an error advance, a two-base hit, or a three-base hit on the wild throw? The advance to third (by_error=5 on the advance) is clear, but whether the primary advance is a hit-type one base or more is ambiguous. Supplied label 'single' is adversarial.
